meta.note: Build artifact: merged from backend/data/cases/*.json. Edit the case files, then rebuild. The Neo4j Aura instance holds the GraphRAG ingestion; this file drives the frontend.

cases.title: The Hummingbird 1:4 Sugar Rule
cases.popular_claim: “Always mix sugar water 1:4 (~20%) — it’s what the science says.”
cases.summary: A feeder rule every site repeats, traced to papers that never prescribed it — while the ~50% sucrose study sits alone, uncited.

cases.title: The 40g Protein Ceiling
cases.popular_claim: “Your body can only absorb ~30–40g of protein per meal — more is wasted.”
cases.summary: A 20g MPS plateau in six young men became a universal digestive ceiling — a 2023 study titled ‘no upper limit’ went ignored.

cases.title: Mount Stupid
cases.popular_claim: “Incompetent people can’t know they’re incompetent — the least skilled are the most overconfident.”
cases.summary: Four small studies and an internet-fabricated curve became ‘a law of psychology’ — random numbers reproduce the curve exactly.

cases.title: The $4 Billion House
cases.popular_claim: “The most expensive house in the world costs $4 billion.”
cases.summary: A compounded projection and a non-saleable palace became a market ‘fact’ — no $4B transaction has ever existed.

cases.title: The 10,000 Steps Commandment
cases.popular_claim: “You need 10,000 steps a day for your health.”
cases.summary: A 1965 pedometer brand’s product name became a clinical commandment — the benefit plateaus thousands of steps lower.

nodes.title: Lessons from Mt. Stupid (the fabricated curve)
nodes.claim: Blog post that paired the Dunning-Kruger name with a peak-and-trough 'Mt. Stupid' curve that appears in no Dunning-Kruger paper.
nodes.note: Earliest known version of the viral curve; the chart, not the studies, is what the culture now cites.

nodes.title: Dunning-Kruger effect (Wikipedia)
nodes.claim: Defines the effect as poor performers' inability to recognize their own incompetence; covers the 1999 study and the later statistical-artifact critiques.
nodes.note: The amplifier: codified the pop-law reading for millions while quietly hosting the critiques.

nodes.title: The Dunning-Kruger Effect: What It Is & Why It Matters
nodes.claim: Mainstream explainer asserting the effect shows incompetent people overestimating their ability; attributes the finding to the 1999 Kruger-Dunning Cornell studies.
nodes.note: Typical SEO health-media echo that converts ~350 undergrads into universal life advice.

nodes.title: Why incompetent people think they're amazing (TED-Ed)
nodes.claim: Animated lesson in which David Dunning himself presents the effect as people frequently overestimating their own abilities.
nodes.note: The origin author laundered the pop version into edutainment for millions of viewers.

nodes.title: The Dunning-Kruger Effect, Explained (Open Culture)
nodes.claim: Pop explainer of the effect that cites no source paper and omits the statistical-artifact critiques entirely.
nodes.note: Shows the mutation in 2024: the 'law' survives with no paper attached.

nodes.title: Unskilled and unaware of it
nodes.claim: Four small studies of ~350 Cornell undergrads: bottom-quartile performers (~12th percentile) self-estimated near the 62nd percentile.
nodes.note: Origin source; its own authors conceded regression to the mean 'virtually guarantees' the pattern and argued only that it was 'more psychological than artifactual.'

nodes.title: Unskilled, unaware, or both?
nodes.claim: Reanalysis showing the apparent miscalibration of low scorers is produced by regression to the mean plus a better-than-average bias, not a metacognitive deficit.
nodes.note: The 2002 kill-shot the pop version of the effect never mentions.

nodes.title: The Dunning-Kruger effect is (mostly) a statistical artefact
nodes.claim: Using a validated signal-detection method in 929 participants, the apparent Dunning-Kruger effect shrinks to '(mostly) a statistical artefact' of measurement conventions.
nodes.note: Largest-sample methodological verdict; cited by the field, ignored by pop media.

nodes.title: A rational model of the Dunning-Kruger effect
nodes.authors: Jansen RA et al. (Nat Hum Behav)
nodes.claim: A computational model plus two studies of roughly 4,000 people finds low performers are less able to tell whether they are correct, reviving a modest genuine metacognitive deficit.
nodes.note: The honest nuance node: not artifact-only, but a far weaker effect than the meme.

nodes.title: The Dunning-Kruger effect and its discontents
nodes.claim: David Dunning defends the effect as a real metacognitive deficit, arguing the artifact critiques misread the data and ignore contrary research.
nodes.note: Even the origin author now defends only a weakened, qualified version.

nodes.title: Random Number Simulations Reveal How Random Noise Affects Self-Assessed Competency
nodes.claim: Random-number data containing no psychology at all, plotted with the field's quartile conventions, reproduce the classic Dunning-Kruger curve exactly.
nodes.note: The killer counter-truth: the curve is an artifact of plotting; essentially nobody cites it.

nodes.title: Look inside the most expensive house in the world
nodes.claim: Calls Buckingham Palace the most expensive house in the world at $4.9 billion, citing no source for the figure, while noting Antilia is worth between $1 billion and $2 billion.
nodes.note: Most-viral mutation: assigns a market price to non-saleable Crown property with no citation.

nodes.title: Inside $4.6 billion home of one of world's richest people
nodes.claim: Repeats that Mukesh Ambani's Antilia is a $4.6 billion home with a snow room, spa, ice cream parlor and 168-car garage, citing no source.
nodes.note: Viral lifestyle piece mirroring the Financial Express headline's exact amenity list while dropping the source.

nodes.title: Most Expensive House in The World 2026
nodes.claim: Ranks Buckingham Palace as the most expensive house in the world at $4.9 billion and gives Antilia a $2-4.6 billion range.
nodes.note: SEO listicle fusing the Fox Buckingham figure with the FE/Wikipedia Antilia figure.

nodes.title: The Most Expensive Houses In The World In 2025
nodes.claim: Lists Buckingham Palace as the most expensive house in the world at $4.9 billion and Antilia at $2 billion.
nodes.note: Listicle repeating the unsourced $4.9B Buckingham tag alongside the real $2B Antilia cost.

nodes.title: What is the Most Expensive House in the World?
nodes.claim: Names Buckingham Palace the most expensive house in the world at $4.9 billion, with Antilia listed at $2 billion, citing no source.
nodes.note: General-knowledge study material canonizing the unsourced Buckingham figure for Indian exam-prep audiences.

nodes.title: Antilia (building) — Wikipedia
nodes.claim: States Antilia is valued at $4.6 billion citing the Financial Express article, while noting its construction cost was almost US$2 billion.
nodes.note: Adopted the FE $4.6B figure (ref tagged '[unreliable source]'); downstream listicles copy-pasted it, some keeping the tag artifact.

nodes.title: Inside Antilia, a $2 billion Mumbai mansion
nodes.claim: Reports Antilia's value as between $1 billion and $2 billion, the real build-cost reporting now circulating alongside the $4.6B myth.
nodes.note: The accurate cost figure presented in the same popular layer; current headline rounds it to $2 billion.

nodes.title: Mukesh Ambani's 4.6 billion 27-story skyscraper home
nodes.claim: Values Mukesh Ambani's 27-storey Mumbai home Antilia at $4.6 billion.
nodes.note: Origin of the number: a projection exercise compounding Mumbai residential price appreciation onto Antilia's ~$1-2B build cost, presented as a market valuation; page is JS-rendered, content verified via Wayback snapshot and Wikipedia's citation of it (19 Apr 2023).

nodes.title: Buckingham Palace listed for sale in spoof advert
nodes.claim: Reports that Buckingham Palace is not actually for sale after Emoov's spoof advert valued it at about £4.9 billion by multiplying £64,831 per square metre across 77,000 m².
nodes.note: Documents the spoof-estimate methodology and the palace's non-saleable status that the $4.9B headlines omit.

nodes.title: $238M Central Park apartment, highest price ever in US
nodes.claim: Ken Griffin's $238 million penthouse at 220 Central Park South was the highest price ever paid for a home in the US, breaking the prior $137 million record.
nodes.note: Verified most expensive US home sale ever; stands in for the paywalled WSJ original (401), verified via CNN syndication.

nodes.title: Russian billionaire loses $54m deposit on world's most expensive home
nodes.claim: Mikhail Prokhorov agreed to buy Villa Leopolda for £360 million but forfeited his $54 million deposit plus $1.5 million interest when he backed out, so the sale never completed.
nodes.note: Lonely court-record fact: even the most famous 'world's most expensive home' sale collapsed at ~£360M — no $4B transaction has ever existed.

nodes.title: Hummingbird Nectar Ratio
nodes.claim: Always mix exactly 1 part sugar to 4 parts water; anything stronger harms the birds.
nodes.note: Absolutizes the 1:4 rule; no primary source.

nodes.title: How Much Sugar Do I Add to 2 Cups of Water?
nodes.claim: The only safe recipe is 1 part sugar to 4 parts water.
nodes.note: Restates 1:4 as settled fact.

nodes.title: Turn Your Yard Into a Hummingbird Spectacular
nodes.claim: Use a 1:4 sugar-water ratio to mimic natural nectar.
nodes.note: Popular authority repeating the ratio.

nodes.title: HIOG #1: Hummingbird Food Preferences
nodes.claim: Cites a 2008 Condor study as support for the ~20% recipe — the anchor mis-citation in this chain.
nodes.note: Entry article we traced; mis-attributes the ratio to McCaffrey & Wethington 2008.

nodes.title: Food Preference by Hummingbirds Visiting Feeders (report)
nodes.claim: Downloadable 2023 report underpinning the Substack post.
nodes.note: One of four verified downloadable sources.

nodes.title: Seeing Fewer Hummingbirds — Should You Worry?
nodes.claim: Repeats the 1:4 recipe as standard guidance.
nodes.note: Authoritative outlet reinforcing the rule.

nodes.title: Here's What to Feed Your Summer Bird-Feeder Visitors
nodes.claim: 1 part sugar to 4 parts water recommended.
nodes.note: Propagation of the ratio.

nodes.title: Feeders in Fall
nodes.claim: Practitioner guidance echoing the 1:4 mix.
nodes.note: Older practitioner page in the chain.

nodes.title: Hummingbird Nectar Recipe
nodes.claim: Official recipe page prescribing 1 part sugar to 4 parts water.
nodes.note: Institutional authority the popular layer points to.

nodes.title: The Hummingbird Book
nodes.claim: Widely-owned popular book stating the 1:4 recipe.
nodes.note: Expert-practice book anchoring later web claims.

nodes.title: Feeding Hummingbirds: The Basics
nodes.claim: Field-guide author's practice page recommending 1:4.
nodes.note: Expert-practice source ('Sheri').

nodes.title: How the Presence of Feeders Affects the Use of Local Floral Resources by Hummingbirds
nodes.claim: A field study on feeders vs. floral resource use — NOT a ratio recommendation, yet repeatedly mis-cited as endorsing ~20%.
nodes.note: The misread anchor. The Condor 110(4):786-791. Verified via Crossref.

nodes.title: Annual Survival & Recruitment in a Ruby-throated Hummingbird Population
nodes.claim: Population survival/recruitment study cited as scientific backing but unrelated to sugar ratio.
nodes.note: One of four verified papers; demographic, not dietary.

nodes.title: Crop Volume, Nectar Concentration & Hummingbird Energetics
nodes.claim: Foundational energetics: intake and efficiency favor more concentrated nectar than 20%.
nodes.note: Foundational, under-cited by the popular layer.

nodes.title: Nectar Concentration Preferences & Intake Rate
nodes.claim: Experimental preference for concentrations well above 20%.
nodes.note: Overlooked primary evidence.

nodes.title: Sugar Preferences & Feeding in Nectarivores
nodes.claim: Preference and physiology support concentrated solutions.
nodes.note: Overlooked primary evidence.

nodes.title: Nectar Foraging Dynamics
nodes.claim: Recent foraging study consistent with higher-concentration preference.
nodes.note: Recent evidence, disconnected from popular chain.

nodes.title: Patterns in Floral Nectar Characteristics (Costa Rica)
nodes.claim: Natural hummingbird-flower nectar spans a wide range, often >20% sugar.
nodes.note: Natural-nectar baseline evidence.

nodes.title: Sugar Assimilation & Digestive Efficiency in Hummingbirds
nodes.claim: Physiology supports efficient use of concentrated nectar.
nodes.note: Overlooked physiological evidence.

nodes.title: Rufous Hummingbird Sucrose Preference: Precision of Selection Varies with Concentration
nodes.claim: Rufous hummingbirds prefer high sucrose concentrations (~50%); selection precision rises with concentration. The isolated, strongest counter-evidence — cited by none of the popular chain.
nodes.note: Standalone endpoint. The Condor 102(1):235-238. Verified via Crossref.

nodes.title: How Much Protein Per Meal (TODAY.com)
nodes.claim: Dietitians tell readers to eat 20-30 g protein per meal (20-40 g if goals are higher), saying the body 'can only absorb and use a certain amount of protein at a time,' the cap is 'up for debate... some research saying 30 grams and other studies saying 40 grams,' and there is 'no reason to eat more than 40 grams at once.'
nodes.note: Most viral mainstream restatement: turns an MPS plateau into a digestive absorb-and-excrete ceiling.

nodes.title: Eat to Build Muscle: Every 3 Hours, 30 g
nodes.claim: Recommends eating every ~3 hours across six meals a day and to 'shoot for about 30 grams of protein per meal' to support muscle growth.
nodes.note: Canonical gym-lore pairing: the 3-hour meal cadence plus a 30 g per-meal cap.

nodes.title: r/ScientificNutrition: Only 20-30 g Absorbed?
nodes.claim: Thread opens with the premise 'If a person can only absorb 20 or 30 grams of protein a time' and asks how bulk eating is even possible - the ceiling repeated as settled fact before debate begins.
nodes.note: The myth as crowdsourced common sense; thread title is itself the mutated claim.

nodes.title: How Much Protein Do You Need Daily? (UnityPoint)
nodes.claim: A dietitian advises metabolizing protein '15-30 grams at a time' because 'studies show a higher intake of protein, like more than 40 grams in one sitting, isn't more beneficial.'
nodes.note: Institutional health authority laundering the ceiling into clinical-sounding guidance.

nodes.title: Protein Dose Response of MPS After Resistance Exercise
nodes.authors: Moore DR et al. (Am J Clin Nutr)
nodes.claim: In 6 young men after leg-only resistance exercise, 20 g whole-egg protein maximally stimulated muscle protein synthesis; 40 g produced no statistically significant further rise (a small ~10-20% bump) but did increase leucine oxidation.
nodes.note: The misread anchor: a leg-exercise MPS plateau in 6 subjects that nobody citing a '30-40 g digestive ceiling' represents faithfully.

nodes.title: How Much Protein Can the Body Use in a Single Meal?
nodes.authors: Schoenfeld BJ & Aragon AA (J Int Soc Sports Nutr)
nodes.claim: Recommends 0.4 g/kg/meal across at least 4 meals (>=1.6 g/kg/day) and argues higher per-meal doses are not all oxidized - explicitly rejecting a hard single-meal utilization ceiling.
nodes.note: The corrective review that keeps the per-meal framing but demolishes the absolute cap.

nodes.title: 40 g vs 20 g Whey After Whole-Body Exercise
nodes.claim: In 30 resistance-trained men after whole-body resistance exercise, 40 g whey stimulated greater muscle protein synthesis than 20 g (0.059 vs 0.049 %/h, P=0.005).
nodes.note: Direct counter-evidence: doubles the 'max useful dose' once whole-body training is used.

nodes.title: 30 g vs 90 g Lean Beef and MPS
nodes.authors: Symons TB et al. (J Am Diet Assoc)
nodes.claim: A 113 g beef serving (30 g protein) raised muscle protein synthesis ~50% in young and elderly adults; a 340 g serving (90 g protein) produced no further increase over 5 h.
nodes.note: The honest nuance the myth omits: a real plateau over 5 h, but for MPS - not an absorption ceiling.

nodes.title: ISSN Position Stand: Protein and Exercise
nodes.authors: Jäger R et al. (J Int Soc Sports Nutr)
nodes.claim: Position stand recommends 1.4-2.0 g/kg/day for most exercising individuals and frames per-meal doses of ~20-40 g as context-dependent rather than a fixed absorption limit.
nodes.note: Society-level synthesis the pop layer never quotes.

nodes.title: How Much Protein Can You Eat in One Sitting?
nodes.claim: Reviews the dose-response literature (Moore 2009, Symons 2009, Macnaughton 2016) and concludes the body can absorb and use well more than 30 g in one sitting - the '30 g max' is a misreading of acute MPS studies.
nodes.note: Lay-friendly debunk the mutated layer ignores; live page bot-blocked during verification (URL real, archived Jan 2025).

nodes.title: No Upper Limit to the Anabolic Response (100 g vs 25 g)
nodes.authors: Trommelen J et al. (Cell Rep Med)
nodes.claim: 100 g milk protein produced a greater and more prolonged (>12 h) anabolic response than 25 g, with amino-acid incorporation rising dose-dependently - the response had 'no upper limit in magnitude and duration' in vivo in humans.
nodes.note: The lonely, ignored endpoint: the only node cited by none of the popular chain - four times the 'max' and the curve was still climbing.

nodes.title: Wikipedia: Pedometer ('10,000 steps')
nodes.claim: Repeats 10,000 steps a day as the standard walking recommendation, documents the origin as Kato's manpo-kei 'ten-thousand step-meter', and notes most health benefit is obtained by around 7,000 steps per day.
nodes.note: Layer-1 amplifier: canonizes the number while quietly embedding its marketing origin; living page (snapshot verified Sep 2026).

nodes.title: How walking 10,000 steps a day changes your body
nodes.claim: Promises body transformations from walking 10,000 steps a day over 3 months while conceding the target was 'a marketing ploy that dates back to a Japanese pedometer brand in the 1960s' and suggesting 7,500 steps may suffice.
nodes.note: Typical modern hype node: debunk caveat in passing, 10,000 kept in the headline and goal.

nodes.title: You Don't Need to Walk 10,000 Steps Every Day
nodes.claim: Reports that 10,000 steps is 'the default daily goal for some of the most popular activity trackers on the market' despite tracing the figure to Yamasa's 1965 marketing pedometer, and notes mortality rates level off at about 7,500 steps.
nodes.note: Names the tracker-default mechanism that cemented the number on millions of wrists.

nodes.title: U of T 10,000 Steps Challenge for Staff
nodes.claim: Month-long staff wellness challenge (May 1-31, 2024, run with Incentfit) in which teams win prizes by averaging 10,000 steps per day.
nodes.note: Workplace-challenge variant: the product number institutionalized as HR wellness policy.

nodes.title: '10,000 Steps Duesseldorf' campaign
nodes.authors: Fialho et al. (Int J Behav Nutr Phys Act)
nodes.claim: Evaluates the '10,000 Steps Duesseldorf' city-wide campaign promoting 10,000 steps/day (627 participants at baseline); intervention participants walked only ~462 more steps/day than controls and rates of actually reaching 10,000 did not differ.
nodes.note: The mutation scaled to municipal policy: a city program named for a pedometer slogan, with no origin science cited.

nodes.title: Yamasa 'Manpo-kei' pedometer
nodes.claim: The 10,000-steps figure began as 'Manpo-kei' (ten-thousand-steps meter), the name of Yamasa's 1965 pedometer launched around the 1964 Tokyo Olympics fitness boom - a marketing slogan, not a scientific finding; Harvard Health confirms 'the name was a marketing tool.'
nodes.note: True origin of the number: a Japanese product name recast worldwide as a clinical commandment (origin documented by Harvard Health, Jul 2019).

nodes.title: Step volume & intensity vs mortality in older women
nodes.authors: Lee IM et al. (JAMA Intern Med)
nodes.claim: Among 16,741 women (mean age 72) wearing accelerometers, more daily steps were associated with lower all-cause mortality until approximately 7,500 steps/day, with no further mortality benefit beyond that point.
nodes.note: First large cohort to show the mortality plateau sits ~25% below the folk target. JAMA Intern Med 2019;179(8):1105-1112.

nodes.title: Daily step count & mortality in US adults (NHANES)
nodes.claim: Among 4,840 US adults aged 40+, a greater daily step count was significantly associated with lower all-cause mortality, with benefit concentrated around 8,000 steps/day versus ~4,000; step intensity was not associated with mortality after adjustment for step volume.
nodes.note: National-sample cohort evidence that the benefit concentrates well below 10,000. JAMA 2020;323(12):1151-1160.

nodes.title: Daily steps & all-cause mortality: 15-cohort meta-analysis
nodes.authors: Paluch E et al. (Lancet Public Health)
nodes.claim: Across 47,471 adults in 15 international cohorts, more steps per day were associated with progressively lower all-cause mortality up to about 6,000-8,000 steps/day for adults aged 60+ and 8,000-10,000 for younger adults, with no special additional benefit at 10,000 itself.
nodes.note: Definitive dose-response meta-analysis: 10,000 was never a threshold. Lancet Public Health 2022;7(3):e219-e228.

nodes.title: Steps per day & mortality in middle age (CARDIA)
nodes.authors: Paluch E et al. (JAMA Netw Open)
nodes.claim: Among 2,110 Black and White men and women aged 38-50 in the CARDIA cohort, taking approximately 7,000 steps/day or more was associated with lower mortality than taking fewer than 7,000, with mortality rates leveling out at higher step counts.
nodes.note: Strong cohort evidence sitting entirely outside the hype chain - cited by none of the popular layer. JAMA Netw Open 2021;4(9):e2124516.
